issues.legal_issue: In an inquiry into whether a religious institution is a public trust, the burden of proving its public character rests on the party asserting that character.
material_facts: The proceeding arose from an application seeking a determination that the institution was private, after which the authorities found it to be a public trust.
No member of the public appeared or gave evidence that the public worshipped there as of right, and the evidence that visitors came with the family’s permission was unchallenged.

Although the Charity Commissioner initially recognized that the burden rested on the party asserting a public trust, the decision ultimately faulted the private claimant for not producing title documents.
issues.conclusion: The Charity Commissioner wrongly shifted the burden of proof to the private claimant; the burden of establishing that a public trust existed lay on the party asserting that it did.
issues.legal_principle: In the proceeding under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, the Court treated the burden of proving the asserted public-trust character as resting on the party making that assertion. Sections 18 and 72 provide the procedural context for the application and reference in this case; the judgment identifies no separate statutory provision as the source of the burden rule.

predicates.public_trust_status_inquiry: A proceeding requires a determination whether a religious institution is a public trust or private property.
predicates.public_trust_character_asserted: A party in the proceeding asserts that the institution is a public trust.

issues.definition: When a proceeding determines an institution’s status and a party asserts that it is a public trust, that party bears the burden of proving the asserted public character.

issues.legal_issue: An institution established as a private family institution remains private unless clear and definite evidence proves a later dedication for public use.
material_facts: The evidence showed that the family’s ancestor built the samadhi and mandir, and there was no evidence that the public built them or contributed funds for their construction.
The institution stood within the family’s residential premises; the shrine occupied a small part of a larger property otherwise used by the family.
The family managed the property, collected its rents, and recorded ownership through family succession; a sanad described the land as private property transferable to heirs.
There was no evidence that the public worshipped as of right. The evidence was consistent with visitors attending by invitation, including during a festival.

Government grants began after the institution had been built and were made for worship and family-associated anniversary functions. The Court found that the grants and the other cited records did not establish a public dedication.
issues.conclusion: The institution was the private property of the family and was not a public trust; the appeal was allowed and the judgment finding it private was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Goswamy Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Ranchhoddas Kalidas, if a temple originated as a public temple, that origin establishes its public character; if it originated as private, or its origin is unknown, evidence of public use is required. A private institution’s character is not effaced without clear and definite evidence of later dedication for public use; visits permitted by the owners may be visits by invitees. The Court also relied on Peesapati v. Kanduri and Devki Nandan v. Murlidhar for considering whether a temple lies within residential quarters or in a separate building. It treated location, the relative size of the shrine, management and title records, and the circumstances of public visits, offerings and grants as relevant evidence.

rule.if: temple_status_dispute and private_origin and not clear_later_public_dedication and family_management_evidence and private_title_evidence

predicates.temple_status_dispute: A proceeding requires a determination whether a temple or math is public or private.
predicates.private_origin: The evidence shows that the institution was established by a family for its own religious purposes rather than by the public.
predicates.clear_later_public_dedication: Clear and definite evidence shows that the owners later dedicated the institution for public use.
predicates.family_management_evidence: The evidence shows that the family managed or used the institution and its surrounding property as family property.
predicates.private_title_evidence: The evidence includes records or other material indicating that the property was privately owned or passed through family succession.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a temple’s status, a private origin, no clear later public dedication, and evidence of family management and private title mean that the institution is private rather than a public trust.
